To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
mixed biofilms composed of emerging microorganisms in CF are more resistant to antimicrobals than monospecies biofilms.
the interactions between emerging and conventional CF pathogens in dual-species mixed biofilms can increase the tolerance of the overall consortium to most antibiotics.
mixed-species biofilms formed by P. aeruginosaa, D. pigruma and I. limosusa were more resistant than monospecies biofilms, with the exception of D. pigrumsusceptible to cefepime.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of emerging bacteria in the development of mixed biofilms and their antibiotic susceptibility patterns.
the development of a better understanding of the complex interactions of the microbial community in CF, which may lead to more effective treatments for CF patients.

the development of new therapeutic approaches for the treatment of infections in CF patients, where the interactions between different bacterial species are crucial to understanding the persistence of the disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the interactions between the emerging species, I. limosu and D. piggum, and the classical CF pathogen P. aeruginos, in mixed biofilm communities, may have an impact on treatment of infection, as they may increase the tolerance of the overall community towards antimicrobial treatment.

the presence of the two emerging species, I. limosum and D. pignum, in dual-species consortia with P. aeroginosa, significantly increases the tolerance of the overall consortium to most antimicrobial agents.

the interactions of the emerging species I limosus and/or D. pigrun with the conventional CF pathogenic species P aeruginosa, may be crucial to understanding persistent colonisation in cystic fibrous (CF) lungs and the development of new therapeutic approaches.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the presence of I. limosu and D. pgrum in biofilm communities with P. aerugionsa increases the tolerance of the consortia to most antimicrobial agents, even without an increase in the number of cells in the biofilm.

the presence of I. limosu and D. piggum in dual-species with P. aerugionsa, in mixed biofilms, increased the tolerance of P. aeruginosas to most antibiotics, including the last resort antibiotic colistin.
the interactions between the emerging species I limosus and the conventional pathogen P. aeruginosawere crucial in increasing tolerance to antimicrobial agents in dual-species CF biofilms.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the presence of I. limosu and D. piggum, in mixed biofilms with Pseudomonas, increases the resistance of the biofilm consortia to antimicrobals, even without an increase in the number of encased cells.
the antibiotic resistance of the mixed biofilms in CF may be impacted by the interactions between emerging microorganisms and classical CF pathogens.
the interactions between different species are crucial for the outcome of biofilms, which may have a significant impact on the development of effective therapies for cystic fibrosis.
